lead: This unit introduces the building blocks of neural networks and shows how they are trained. After reading, the student can design a simple feed‑forward network, train it with back‑propagation, and explain the role of deep and convolutional architectures.
about: Unit 5 consists of nine chapters. Chapter 5.1 starts with the biological neuron and the McCulloch‑Pitts model. Chapter 5.2 adds the perceptron learning rule and its limits. Chapter 5.3 builds multilayer feed‑forward networks with hidden layers. Chapter 5.4 discusses activation and loss functions. Chapter 5.5 derives back‑propagation. Chapter 5.6 covers gradient‑based optimizers and regularisation. Chapter 5.7 compares shallow and deep networks. Chapter 5.8 explains convolution and pooling in CNNs. Chapter 5.9 introduces recurrent networks. Each chapter builds on the previous one and links to earlier units on basic learning concepts and model evaluation.

chapters.idea: A neuron can be modelled as a binary threshold unit.
chapters.depth: Explain the anatomy of a biological neuron, then define the McCulloch‑Pitts (MP) model: weighted sum, threshold θ, binary output. Mention that some syllabi call it the MP model. Keep algebra to a single equation.

figure.title: MP neuron
figure.aria: Shows inputs weighted, summed, compared to threshold, and binary output.

chapters.trap: Forgetting the bias term (θ) when computing the output.

chapters.idea: The perceptron learns linear decision boundaries.
chapters.depth: Present the perceptron update Δw = η (t‑y) x, learning rate η, and convergence theorem for linearly separable data. Note that some syllabi list a single‑layer perceptron. Mention the XOR limitation as a reason for deeper networks.

figure.title: Perceptron learning
figure.aria: Shows forward computation and backward error feedback that updates the weights.

chapters.trap: Assuming the perceptron can solve the XOR problem.

chapters.depth: Describe a feed‑forward network with an input layer, one hidden layer, and an output layer. Define hidden units as perceptrons with bias. Use the term MLP as found in syllabi. Briefly note the universal approximation property.

figure.title: Two‑layer network
figure.aria: Shows data flow from input through hidden to output.

chapters.example: Weights: w₁₁=0.6, w₁₂=‑0.4 to hidden1; w₂₁=0.3, w₂₂=0.8 to hidden2; hidden bias=‑0.1; output weight=1.0, bias=0.2. Input (1,0) → hidden sum1=0.6‑0.1=0.5 → step=1; sum2=‑0.4‑0.1=‑0.5 → step=0; output sum=1·1+0·0+0.2=1.2 → step=1.
chapters.trap: Omitting the bias term for each layer.
chapters.leave: Choice of activation functions and loss definitions.

chapters.idea: Activation and loss functions give networks learning power.
chapters.depth: Cover sigmoid, tanh, ReLU, Softmax and their derivatives. Explain mean‑squared error and cross‑entropy loss. Note ReLU and Softmax appear in many syllabi. Add Swish as an optional advanced function (added).

figure.aria: Shows the shapes of sigmoid, tanh and ReLU activation curves.

chapters.example: True class vector t=[0,1]; predicted softmax p=[0.3,0.7]. Cross‑entropy loss = - Σ t_i log(p_i) = -log(0.7)=0.357.
chapters.trap: Using the sigmoid output range in a cross‑entropy formula that expects probabilities from Softmax.

chapters.depth: Derive the error signal δ for output units, propagate δ to hidden units using the chain rule, and update weights with gradient descent. Use terminology “error back propagation” from syllabi. Show vector form.

figure.title: Back‑propagation
figure.aria: Shows forward computation followed by backward error propagation.

chapters.example: Network from Chapter 3, input (1,0), target 0, learning rate η=0.1. Forward gives y=1. Error δ_out = (y‑t)·f' = (1‑0)·1 =1. Hidden δ₁ = w_out·δ_out·f' =1·1·1=1. Weight update w₁←w₁‑η·δ₁·x₁ =0.6‑0.1·1·1=0.5.
chapters.trap: Skipping the derivative of the hidden activation when computing δ for hidden units.

chapters.idea: Optimizers and regularisation improve training stability.
chapters.depth: Define batch GD, stochastic GD, momentum (v←βv+η∇J), RMSProp, Adam (advanced) and weight‑decay L2. Explain dropout and batch‑normalisation (added). Mention that only a few universities cover Adam in depth.

figure.title: Optimizer block
figure.aria: Shows gradient flowing into momentum term and then updating the weights.

chapters.trap: Applying weight‑decay after the gradient step and using the same η for both.
chapters.leave: Why depth matters and how it changes learning dynamics.

chapters.idea: Depth creates hierarchical feature learning and new challenges.
chapters.depth: Compare a shallow MLP (one hidden layer) with a deep network (many hidden layers). Discuss vanishing gradient (unit saturation) and how ReLU mitigates it. Note that only a few universities treat the vanishing‑gradient problem in detail (advanced).

figure.aria: Shows a deep stack of layers from input to output.

chapters.example: Gradient at output =0.8. Using sigmoid, each layer multiplies by 0.5 → after three hidden layers gradient =0.8·0.5³=0.1 (vanishes). With ReLU derivative =1 → gradient stays 0.8.
chapters.trap: Assuming more layers automatically improve accuracy without regularisation.
chapters.leave: Specific deep architectures such as CNNs.

chapters.idea: Convolution and pooling extract spatial features efficiently.
chapters.depth: Define discrete convolution: (x∗k)[i]= Σ x[i+s]·k[s] with stride and padding. Explain max‑pooling and average‑pooling. Cite LeNet, AlexNet, VGG from syllabi. Add dilated convolution as an advanced optional (added).

figure.title: 1‑D convolution example
figure.aria: Shows sliding of a kernel over an input vector, the resulting feature map, and a subsequent max‑pooling step.

chapters.trap: Flipping the kernel when performing convolution; many treat it as cross‑correlation.

chapters.idea: Recurrent networks process ordered data with internal memory.
chapters.depth: Describe a simple RNN cell: h_t = f(W_x x_t + W_h h_{t‑1} + b). Explain unfolding in time and back‑propagation through time. Mention LSTM as listed in syllabi and GRU as an advanced optional (added).

figure.aria: Shows the flow of inputs and hidden states through two time steps of an unfolded RNN.

chapters.trap: Treating each time step as an independent feed‑forward network and not sharing weights.
chapters.leave: Advanced sequence models such as Transformers.
